translations.idiomatic: Ke, because Kang had disobeyed his instruction, then executed him as a warning to others.

sentences.zh: 民聞伉坐執人被戮，知官惟欲出之而已，於是老幼相攜而出，歲期人數，皆如本規。

translations.literal: When the people heard that Kang had been put to death for seizing and killing a surrendered man, they knew the officials wanted only to get them out; thereupon old and young led one another forth, and by year's end the numbers of people matched the original plan.
translations.idiomatic: When the people heard that Kang had been put to death for seizing and killing a surrendered man, they knew the officials wanted only to get them out; thereupon old and young led one another forth, and by year's end the numbers of people matched the original plan.

sentences.zh: 恪自領萬人，餘分給諸將。

translations.literal: Ke himself commanded ten thousand men; the remainder he divided among the various generals.
translations.idiomatic: Ke himself commanded ten thousand men; the remainder he divided among the various generals.

sentences.zh: 吳主嘉其功，拜恪威北將軍，封都鄉侯，徙屯廬江皖口。

translations.literal: The ruler of Wu praised his achievement, appointed Ke General Who Establishes Might in the North, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Duxiang, and transferred his encampment to Wankou in Lujiang.
translations.idiomatic: The ruler of Wu praised his achievement, appointed Ke General Who Establishes Might in the North, enfeoffed him as Marquis of Duxiang, and transferred his encampment to Wankou in Lujiang.

sentences.zh: 是歲，徙長安鐘虡、橐佗、銅人、承露盤於洛陽。

translations.literal: That year, the bell stands, the stone chimes, the bronze men, and the Dew Collecting Basin were moved from Chang'an to Luoyang.
translations.idiomatic: That year, the bell stands, the stone chimes, the bronze men, and the Dew Collecting Basin were moved from Chang'an to Luoyang.

sentences.zh: 盤折，聲聞數十里。

translations.literal: The basin broke, and the sound was heard for several tens of li.
translations.idiomatic: The basin broke, and the sound was heard for several tens of li.

sentences.zh: 銅人重，不可致，留於霸城。

translations.literal: The bronze men were too heavy to be moved and were left at Bawu.
translations.idiomatic: The bronze men were too heavy to be moved and were left at Bawu.

sentences.zh: 大發銅鑄銅人二，號曰翁仲，列坐於司馬門外。

translations.literal: Copper was cast on a great scale to make two bronze men, called Wengzhong, and they were set in rows outside the Sima Gate.
translations.idiomatic: Copper was cast on a great scale to make two bronze men, called Wengzhong, and they were set in rows outside the Sima Gate.

sentences.zh: 又鑄黃龍、鳳皇各一，龍高四丈，鳳高三太餘，置內殿前。

translations.literal: Yellow dragons and phoenixes were also cast, one of each; the dragon was four zhang high, the phoenix more than three zhang high, and they were placed before the inner hall.
translations.idiomatic: Yellow dragons and phoenixes were also cast, one of each; the dragon was four zhang high, the phoenix more than three zhang high, and they were placed before the inner hall.

sentences.zh: 起土山於芳林園西北陬，使公卿群僚皆負土，樹松、竹、雜木、善草於其上，捕山禽雜獸致其中。

translations.literal: An earthen hill was raised in the northwest corner of the Fanglin Garden; he made the chief ministers and the host of officials all carry earth, and planted pines, bamboo, miscellaneous trees, and fine grasses upon it, and captured mountain birds and assorted beasts and placed them within.
translations.idiomatic: An earthen hill was raised in the northwest corner of the Fanglin Garden; he made the chief ministers and the host of officials all carry earth, and planted pines, bamboo, miscellaneous trees, and fine grasses upon it, and captured mountain birds and assorted beasts and placed them within.

sentences.zh: 司徒軍議掾董尋上疏諫曰：「臣聞古之直士，盡言於國，不避死亡，故周昌比高祖於桀、紂，劉輔譬趙后於人婢。

translations.literal: Dong Xun, military planning aide to the Grand Minister, submitted a remonstrance, saying: "I have heard that the upright men of old spoke their full mind to the state and did not shun death; therefore Zhou Chang compared Gaozu to Jie and Zhou, and Liu Fu likened Empress Zhao to a serving maid."
translations.idiomatic: Dong Xun, military planning aide to the Grand Minister, submitted a remonstrance, saying, "I have heard that the upright men of old spoke their full mind to the state and did not shun death; therefore Zhou Chang compared Gaozu to Jie and Zhou, and Liu Fu likened Empress Zhao to a serving maid."

sentences.zh: 天生忠直，雖白刃沸湯，往而不顧者，誠為時主愛惜天下也。

translations.literal: Heaven produces loyalty and uprightness; though white blades and boiling water lie ahead, they go forward without turning back—truly because they cherish the realm under the ruler of the age.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven produces loyalty and uprightness; though white blades and boiling water lie ahead, they go forward without turning back—truly because they cherish the realm under the ruler of the age.

sentences.zh: 建安以來，野戰死亡，或門殫戶盡，雖有存者，遺孤老弱。

translations.literal: Since the Jian'an era, deaths in field battle have left some families extinguished door to door; even where survivors remain, they are orphaned, aged, and weak.
translations.idiomatic: Since Jian'an, battle after battle has emptied whole households; where anyone still lives, it is the orphaned, the aged, and the helpless.

sentences.zh: 若今宮室狹小，當廣大之，猶宜隨時，不妨農務，況乃作無益之物！

translations.literal: If the palace halls are narrow today, they should be enlarged—yet even that should suit the times and not hinder farm work, to say nothing of making useless things!
translations.idiomatic: If the halls are cramped, enlarge them—but in season, without disturbing the harvest. How much less should you raise things of no use!

sentences.zh: 黃龍、鳳皇、九龍、承露盤，此皆聖明之所不興也，其功三倍於殿捨。

translations.literal: Yellow dragons, phoenixes, Nine Dragons, the Dew Collecting Basin—these are things no sage ruler would raise; their labor is three times that of palace buildings.
translations.idiomatic: Yellow dragons, phoenixes, the Nine Dragons, the Dew Collecting Basin—no enlightened sovereign would build such things; their cost is triple that of halls and chambers.

sentences.zh: 陛下既尊群臣，顯以冠冕，被以文繡，載以華輿，所以異於小人；

translations.literal: Your Majesty already honors your ministers, making them conspicuous with caps and crowns, draping them in patterned brocade, and bearing them in splendid carriages—thereby distinguishing them from commoners;
translations.idiomatic: You already exalt your ministers with caps and crowns, brocade robes, and splendid carriages, setting them apart from common men;

sentences.zh: 而使穿方舉土，面目垢黑，沾體塗足，衣冠了鳥，毀國之光以崇無益，甚非謂也。

translations.literal: yet you make them dig squares and haul earth until their faces are black with grime, their bodies and feet smeared with mud, their robes and caps ruined—a blot on the state's glory to exalt the useless. This is very far from what should be.
translations.idiomatic: yet you set them to dig and haul earth until their faces are black, their limbs caked in mud, their dress in tatters—dimming the nation's luster to glorify what is worthless. This is not what should be done.

sentences.zh: 孔子曰：『君使臣以禮，臣事君以忠。

translations.literal: Confucius said: "The ruler employs his ministers with ritual; ministers serve their ruler with loyalty.
translations.idiomatic: Confucius said, "The ruler treats his ministers with ritual; ministers serve their ruler with loyalty.

sentences.zh: 』無忠無禮，國何以立！

translations.literal: " Without loyalty and without ritual, how can the state stand!
translations.idiomatic: Without loyalty and ritual, how can a state endure?

sentences.zh: 臣知言出必死，而臣自比於牛之一毛，生既無益，死亦何損！

translations.literal: I know that once these words leave my mouth I must die; yet I compare myself to a single hair on an ox—living I am of no use; what loss is there in dying?
translations.idiomatic: I know these words will cost me my life; yet I am but one hair on an ox—useless alive, what harm in dying?

sentences.zh: 秉筆流涕，心與世辭。

translations.literal: Holding the brush, I weep; my heart takes leave of the world.
translations.idiomatic: Brush in hand, I weep; my heart has already left this world.

sentences.zh: 臣有八子，臣死之後，累陛下矣！

translations.literal: I have eight sons; after I die, they will burden Your Majesty!
translations.idiomatic: I have eight sons; when I am gone, they will become Your Majesty's burden!

sentences.zh: 」將奏，沐浴以待命。

translations.literal: " When about to submit it, he bathed and awaited the imperial command.
translations.idiomatic: When he was ready to submit the memorial, he bathed and waited for the emperor's word.

sentences.zh: 帝曰：「董尋不畏死邪！

translations.literal: The emperor said: "Dong Xun does not fear death, does he!
translations.idiomatic: The emperor said, "Does Dong Xun not fear death?

sentences.zh: 」主者奏收尋，有詔勿問。

translations.literal: " The chief attendant memorialized to have Xun arrested; an edict came: do not pursue the matter.
translations.idiomatic: The chief attendant moved to arrest Xun; an edict followed: let the matter drop.

sentences.zh: 高堂隆上疏曰：「今之小人，好說秦、漢之奢靡以蕩聖心；

translations.literal: Gao Tanglong submitted a memorial, saying: "The petty men of today love to speak of the extravagance of Qin and Han to unsettle the sage heart;
translations.idiomatic: Gao Tanglong submitted a memorial: "Petty men today praise Qin and Han extravagance to sway Your Majesty's heart;

sentences.zh: 求取亡國不度之器，勞役費損以傷德政。

translations.literal: they seek the implements of doomed states, and by forced labor and wasted expense they injure virtuous government.
translations.idiomatic: they demand the trappings of fallen dynasties, wasting labor and treasure and wounding good rule.

sentences.zh: 非所以興禮樂之和，保神明之休也。

translations.literal: This is not the way to raise the harmony of ritual and music and preserve the repose of the spirits.
translations.idiomatic: This is no way to foster ritual and music, or to keep heaven and the ancestral spirits at peace.

sentences.zh: 」帝不聽。

translations.literal: " The emperor did not heed it.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor would not listen.

sentences.zh: 隆又上書曰：「昔洪水滔天二十二載，堯、舜君臣南面而已。

translations.literal: Long again submitted a memorial, saying: "In olden days the floodwaters rose for twenty-two years, yet Yao and Shun, ruler and ministers, merely faced south and that was all.
translations.idiomatic: Long wrote again: "When the great flood raged for twenty-two years, Yao and Shun and their ministers did nothing but face south.

sentences.zh: 今無若時之急，而使公卿大夫並與廝徒共供事役，聞之四夷，非嘉聲也，垂之竹帛，非令名也。

translations.literal: Today there is no urgency like that of those times, yet you make chief ministers and grandees share forced labor with menials and runners; if the four barbarians hear of it, it is no fine report, and if it is handed down on bamboo and silk, it is no good name.
translations.idiomatic: Today there is no such crisis, yet nobles and clerks toil beside common laborers. If the four quarters hear of it, it will not sound well; if it is written into history, it will not be a name to cherish.

sentences.zh: 今吳、蜀二賊，非徒白地、小虜、聚邑之寇，乃僭號稱帝，欲與中國爭衡。

translations.literal: The two bandits Wu and Shu are not mere empty lands, petty raiders, or brigands of clustered hamlets—they have usurped imperial titles and would contend with the Central State.
translations.idiomatic: Wu and Shu are no empty borderlands or petty raiders—they have crowned themselves and would rival the Middle Kingdom.

sentences.zh: 今若有人來告：『權、禪並修德政，輕省租賦，動咨耆賢，事遵禮度，』陛下聞之，豈不惕然惡其如此，以為難卒討滅而為國憂乎！

translations.literal: If someone now came to report: "Sun Quan and Liu Shan both cultivate virtue, lighten taxes and levies, consult the aged and worthy, and conduct affairs according to ritual and measure," would Your Majesty not, on hearing it, shudder and hate that they were so, deeming them hard to destroy at once and a worry to the state!
translations.idiomatic: Suppose word came that Sun Quan and Liu Shan were practicing virtue, easing taxes, seeking counsel from elders, and keeping to ritual—would you not shudder at their strength and fear they would be hard to crush?

sentences.zh: 若使告者曰：『彼二賊並為無道，崇侈無度，役其士民，重其賦斂，下不堪命，吁嗟日甚，』陛下聞之，豈不幸彼疲敝而取之不難乎！

translations.literal: If the reporter said: "Those two bandits are both without the Way, exalting extravagance without limit, driving their people in forced labor, and heaping taxes and levies upon them until the lower orders cannot endure it and their cries of woe grow daily," would Your Majesty not, on hearing it, rejoice that they are worn out and that taking them would not be hard!
translations.idiomatic: Suppose instead he said they were lawless, extravagant, crushing their people with labor and taxes until the realm groaned—would you not rejoice that they were weakening and easy to overcome?

sentences.zh: 苟如此，則可易心而度，事義之數亦不遠矣！

translations.literal: If it is so, then one may change one's heart and measure accordingly—the numbers of affairs and right principle are not far off!
translations.idiomatic: If you can think thus, you can read their hearts and act accordingly—the right course is not far to seek.

sentences.zh: 亡國這主自謂不亡，然後至於亡；

translations.literal: Lords of doomed states deem themselves not doomed—and only then come to ruin;
translations.idiomatic: The lord of a falling state thinks himself secure—and only then does ruin come;

sentences.zh: 賢聖之君自謂亡，然後至於不亡。

translations.literal: sage rulers deem themselves on the brink of ruin—and only then do they not perish.
translations.idiomatic: The sage ruler thinks himself already lost—and only then does the state endure.

sentences.zh: 今天下雕敝，民無儋石之儲，國無終年之蓄，外有強敵，六軍暴邊，內興土功，州郡騷動，若有寇警，則臣懼版築之士不能投命虜庭矣。

translations.literal: Today the realm is wasted, the people have no store of a dan and a stone, the state has no year's reserve, outside are strong enemies and the Six Armies stand exposed on the frontier, inside you raise earthworks and the commanderies and districts are in turmoil—if an alarm of raiders comes, I fear the men at the ramparts will not be able to give their lives against the barbarian court.
translations.idiomatic: The land is exhausted; families lack even a stone of grain; the treasury holds no year's supply. Enemies press the borders while the Six Armies stand exposed; at home you stir up works and the provinces are in uproar. At the first alarm, I fear the men on the walls will not die for you against the foe.

sentences.zh: 又，將吏奉祿，稍見折減，方之於昔，五分居一，諸受休者又絕稟賜，不應輸者今皆出半，此為官入兼多於舊，其所出與參少於昔。

translations.literal: Moreover, the salaries of generals and officials have been gradually reduced; compared with former times, they are one part in five, and those receiving retirement stipends have also lost their grain grants; those who should not pay levies now pay half—thus official income is greater than before in aggregate, while what is paid out to the ranks is less than before.
translations.idiomatic: Officers' pay has been cut again and again—today it is a fifth of what it once was. Retirees have lost their grain allotments; those once exempt now pay half. Revenue taken in exceeds the old totals, yet what goes out to the ranks falls short.

sentences.zh: 而度支經用，更每不足，牛肉小賦，前後相繼。

translations.literal: Yet the expenditures of the Department of Revenue are more often insufficient, and petty levies on cattle and meat follow one after another.
translations.idiomatic: Still the treasury runs short, and petty taxes on cattle and meat follow one upon another.

sentences.zh: 反而推之，凡此諸費，必有所在。

translations.literal: Work it back the other way—all these expenditures must have their source somewhere.
translations.idiomatic: Reason backward from this: every one of these costs must come from somewhere.

sentences.zh: 且夫祿賜谷帛，人主所以惠養吏民而為之司命者也，若今有廢，是奪其命矣。

translations.literal: Moreover, salaries, grants, grain, and cloth are what the ruler uses to nourish and care for officials and people and to be their arbiter of life; if they are now abolished, that is to seize their very lives.
translations.idiomatic: Salaries, grain, and cloth are how a ruler feeds his officials and people and holds their lives in his hand. To revoke them is to snatch away their very breath.

sentences.zh: 既得之而又失之，此生怨之府也。

translations.literal: Having given and then taking away—this is the storehouse that breeds resentment.
translations.idiomatic: To grant and then withdraw—that is a treasury of resentment.

sentences.zh: 」帝覽之，謂中書監、令曰：「觀隆此奏，使朕懼哉！

translations.literal: " When the emperor read it, he said to the Director and Deputy Director of the Secretariat: "Reading Long's memorial makes me afraid!
translations.idiomatic: When the emperor had read it, he told the Secretariat, "Long's memorial frightens me!

sentences.zh: 尚書衛覬上疏曰：「今議者多好悅耳：其言政治，則比陛下於堯、舜；

translations.literal: Minister of the Masters of Writing Wei Ji submitted a memorial, saying: "Those who debate today mostly love what pleases the ear: in speaking of government, they compare Your Majesty to Yao and Shun;
translations.idiomatic: Wei Ji, Minister of the Masters of Writing, wrote: "Counsellors today flatter the ear. Speak of government, and they liken you to Yao and Shun;

sentences.zh: 其言征伐，則比二虜於狸鼠。

translations.literal: in speaking of campaigns, they compare the two bandits to raccoon-dogs and rats.
translations.idiomatic: speak of war, and they call Wu and Shu no more than rats and foxes.

sentences.zh: 臣以為不然。

translations.literal: I do not think it is so.
translations.idiomatic: I do not believe it.

sentences.zh: 四海之內，分而為三，群士陳力，各為其主，是與六國分治無以為異也。

translations.literal: Within the four seas, the realm is divided in three; scholars exert their strength, each serving his own lord—this is no different from the Six States dividing rule among themselves.
translations.idiomatic: The realm is split three ways; every able man serves his own master. This is no different from the Warring States.

sentences.zh: 當今千里無煙，遺民困苦。

translations.literal: Today for a thousand li there is no smoke of hearth fires; the remnant people are in bitter distress.
translations.idiomatic: For a thousand li the land lies smokeless; the surviving people are in misery.

sentences.zh: 陛下不善留意，將遂凋敝，難可復振。

translations.literal: If Your Majesty does not attend to this with care, the realm will wither and be hard to revive.
translations.idiomatic: If Your Majesty does not heed this, the state will sicken beyond recovery.

sentences.zh: 武皇帝之時，後宮食不過一肉，衣不用錦繡，茵蓐不緣飾，器物無丹漆，用能平定天下，遺福子孫，此皆陛下之所覽也。

translations.literal: In the time of Emperor Wu, food in the rear palace was never more than one dish of meat, clothes were not of brocade or embroidery, mats and bedding had no ornamental borders, and vessels had no cinnabar or lacquer—by this he was able to settle the realm and leave blessing to his descendants; these are things Your Majesty has seen for himself.
translations.idiomatic: Under Emperor Wu of Wei, the inner palace ate but one dish of meat, wore no brocade, used unadorned mats, and kept undecorated vessels—yet he pacified the realm and left fortune to his heirs. Your Majesty has read this history.

sentences.zh: 當今之務，宜君臣上下，計校府庫，量入為出，猶恐不及；

translations.literal: The task of the present day is that ruler and ministers, high and low, should reckon the storehouses and treasuries and measure outgo by income—and even so one may fear it will not suffice;
translations.idiomatic: Today's task is for court and country to count every storehouse, measure every outlay against income—and even then you may fall short;

sentences.zh: 而工役不輟，侈靡日崇，帑藏日竭。

translations.literal: yet forced labor does not cease, extravagance grows daily, and the treasury is drained day by day.
translations.idiomatic: yet labor never stops, luxury mounts daily, and the coffers drain away.

sentences.zh: 昔漢武信神仙之道，謂當得雲表之露以餐玉屑，故立仙掌以承高露，陛下能明，每所非笑。

translations.literal: Formerly Han Wudi believed in the way of immortals, thinking he would obtain dew from above the clouds to eat with jade dust; therefore he set up the Immortal's Palm to catch high dew—Your Majesty is enlightened and has often laughed at this.
translations.idiomatic: Han Wudi sought immortals and built the bronze palm to catch heaven's dew—Your Majesty, being clear-sighted, has often mocked this.

sentences.zh: 漢武有求於露而猶尚見非，陛下無求於露而空設之，不益於好而糜費功夫，誠皆聖慮所宜裁製也。

translations.literal: Han Wudi had a use for the dew and still deserved censure; Your Majesty has no use for dew and yet sets it up empty—not adding to what you love while wasting labor and expense—truly this is what the sage mind ought to cut short.
translations.idiomatic: Wudi at least wanted the dew; you want nothing from it and still build it—no gain, only wasted toil. A wise ruler would put a stop to this.

sentences.zh: 時有詔錄奪士女前已嫁為吏民妻者，還以配士，聽以生口自贖，又簡選其有姿首者內之掖庭。

translations.literal: At this time there was an edict to register and seize gentlewomen and women who had already been married to officials and commoners as wives, to reassign them to soldiers; they were permitted to redeem themselves with captives, and those of comely appearance were selected for the inner quarters.
translations.idiomatic: An edict then ordered the seizure of women already married to officials and commoners for reassignment to soldiers, allowing ransom with captives of matching age and looks—and the fairest were sent to the inner palace.

sentences.zh: 太子舍人沛國張茂上書諫曰：「陛下，天之子也，百姓吏民，亦陛下子也，今奪彼以與此，亦無以異於奪兄之髮妻弟也，於父母之恩偏矣，又，詔書聽得以生口年紀、顏色與妻相當者自代，故富者則傾家盡產，貧者舉假貸貰，貴買生口以贖其妻。

translations.literal: Zhang Mao, Palace Attendant to the Heir Apparent from Pei, submitted a remonstrance, saying: "Your Majesty is Heaven's son, and the common people and officials are also Your Majesty's children; to seize from these and give to those is no different from seizing an elder brother's wife for a younger brother—in partiality to the parents' favor. Moreover, the edict permits redemption with captives matched in age and appearance to one's wife, so the rich exhaust family and estate, the poor borrow and buy on credit, and pay dearly for captives to redeem their wives.
translations.idiomatic: Zhang Mao of Pei, an attendant to the crown prince, remonstrated: "Your Majesty is Heaven's son, and the people are your children. To take wives from some and give them to others is like stealing an elder brother's wife for a younger—an offense against parental justice. The edict lets men ransom their wives with captives of like age and face, so the rich ruin their houses and the poor go into debt to buy slaves for ransom.

sentences.zh: 縣官以配士為名而實內之掖庭，其醜惡乃出與士。

translations.literal: The county office, in the name of assigning wives to soldiers, in fact sent the fair ones to the inner quarters; the ugly ones alone were given out to soldiers.
translations.idiomatic: The counties claim to assign wives to soldiers, but the fair ones go to the inner palace and only the homely are passed to the ranks.

sentences.zh: 得婦者未必喜而失妻者必有憂，或窮或愁，皆不得志。

translations.literal: Those who gained wives were not necessarily glad, while those who lost wives were sure to grieve—some in poverty, some in sorrow, all without satisfaction.
translations.idiomatic: Men who gain wives may not rejoice; men who lose them must grieve—some ruined, some broken, none at peace.

sentences.zh: 夫君有天下而不得萬姓之歡心者，鮮不危殆。

translations.literal: When a ruler possesses the realm yet cannot win the hearts of the myriad people, rarely is he not in peril.
translations.idiomatic: A ruler who holds the realm yet cannot win the people's hearts seldom escapes danger.

sentences.zh: 且軍師在外數十萬人，一日之費非徒千金，舉天下之曲以奉此役，猶將不給，況復有宮庭非員無錄之女。

translations.literal: Moreover, the armies abroad number several hundreds of thousands; the cost of a single day is not merely a thousand in gold—raising the revenue of the whole realm to supply this service still barely suffices, to say nothing of there being unregistered women in the palace beyond quota.
translations.idiomatic: Armies abroad number in the hundreds of thousands; a day's cost runs to more than a thousand in gold. The whole realm's revenue barely feeds the war—how much less can it feed unregistered women in the palace?

sentences.zh: 椒房母后之家，賞賜橫與，內外交引，其費半軍。

translations.literal: In the chambers of consorts and in the households of empresses and queens, rewards are showered without measure; inside and outside offices interlink, and their expense equals half the army.
translations.idiomatic: Consorts and empresses' kin receive boundless gifts; court and kin trade favors, and their cost equals half the army's.

sentences.zh: 昔漢武帝掘地為海，封土為山，賴是時天下為一，莫敢與爭者耳。

translations.literal: Formerly Han Wudi dug the earth into a sea and piled earth into mountains—but then the realm was one and none dared contend with him.
translations.idiomatic: Han Wudi dug seas and piled mountains—but then the empire was whole and none could resist him.

sentences.zh: 自衰亂以來，四五十載，馬不捨鞍，士不釋甲，強寇在疆，圖危魏室。

translations.literal: Since the age of decay and disorder, forty or fifty years have passed; horses have not left the saddle, soldiers have not doffed armor, strong enemies are on the borders, and they plot peril to Wei's house.
translations.idiomatic: For forty or fifty years since the fall, horses have not left the saddle nor soldiers their armor; enemies press the borders and plot Wei's ruin.

sentences.zh: 陛下不戰戰業業，念崇節約，而乃奢靡是務，中尚方作玩弄之物，後園建承露之盤，斯誠快耳目之觀，然亦足以騁寇讎之心矣！

translations.literal: Your Majesty should be cautious and diligent, mindful to honor frugality—yet you make extravagance your task, the Inner Workshop crafts playthings, and the rear garden builds a Dew Collecting Basin; this is indeed a delight to eye and ear, yet it is also enough to unleash the hearts of enemy foes!
translations.idiomatic: You should tremble and practice thrift—yet you chase luxury, the Inner Workshop makes toys, and the rear garden raises a Dew Basin. It pleases the eye, but it also feeds the enemy's hope!

sentences.zh: 惜乎，捨堯、舜之節儉而為漢武帝之侈事，臣竊為陛下不取也。

translations.literal: Alas—to cast aside the frugality of Yao and Shun and take up the extravagance of Han Wudi: I privately deem it unworthy of Your Majesty.
translations.idiomatic: Alas—to abandon Yao and Shun's thrift for Han Wudi's excess: I cannot think it worthy of you.

sentences.zh: 」帝不聽。

translations.literal: " The emperor did not heed it.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor would not listen.

sentences.zh: 高堂隆疾篤，口佔上疏曰：「曾子有言曰：『人之將死，其言也善。

translations.literal: Gao Tanglong, gravely ill, dictated a final memorial, saying: "Zengzi had a saying: 'When a man is about to die, his words are good.'"
translations.idiomatic: Gao Tanglong, near death, dictated a memorial: "Zengzi said, 'When a man is about to die, his words are good.'"

sentences.zh: 』臣寢疾有增無損，常恐奄忽，忠款不昭，臣之丹誠，願陛下少垂省覽！

translations.literal: " My illness grows worse without relief; I constantly fear sudden collapse, and my loyal purpose may not be made clear—my red heart of devotion: I pray Your Majesty will briefly look upon it!
translations.idiomatic: My sickness only worsens. I fear I may die before my loyalty is known—yet I beg Your Majesty to read these words!

sentences.zh: 臣觀三代之有天下，聖賢相承，歷數百載，尺土莫非其有，一民莫非其臣。

translations.literal: I observe that the Three Dynasties possessed the realm: sages and worthies succeeded one another for several hundred years; not a foot of earth was not theirs, not a single subject was not their subject.
translations.idiomatic: The Three Dynasties held the realm for centuries; sage succeeded sage; every inch of land and every soul was theirs.

sentences.zh: 然癸、辛之徒，縱心極欲，皇天震怒，宗國為墟，紂梟白旗，桀放鳴條，天子之尊，湯、武有之。

translations.literal: Yet men like Gui and Xin indulged their hearts to the utmost; High Heaven was angered, their ancestral states became ruins, Zhou of Shang was displayed on a white flag, Jie of Xia was exiled to Mingtiao—the dignity of Son of Heaven, Tang and Wu possessed it.
translations.idiomatic: Yet Jie and Zhou gave free rein to desire; Heaven raged, their houses fell to dust. Zhou died beneath a white flag; Jie was driven to Mingtiao. Even the Son of Heaven's throne passed to Tang and Wu.

sentences.zh: 豈伊異人？

translations.literal: Were they men of another kind?
translations.idiomatic: Were they a different breed of man?

sentences.zh: 皆明王之冑也。

translations.literal: All were descendants of enlightened kings.
translations.idiomatic: They were all heirs of sage kings.

sentences.zh: 黃初之際，天兆其戒，異類之鳥，育長燕巢口爪胸赤，此魏室之大異也。

translations.literal: At the beginning of Huangchu, Heaven showed its warning: a bird of strange kind, reared in a swallow's nest, with red beak, claws, and breast—this was a great anomaly for Wei's house.
translations.idiomatic: At the dawn of Huangchu, Heaven sent a warning: a strange bird, nursed in a swallow's nest, red of beak, claw, and breast—a great omen for Wei.

sentences.zh: 宜防鷹揚之臣於蕭牆之內。

translations.literal: You should guard against hawk-keen ministers within the inner court.
translations.idiomatic: Guard against fierce ministers within your own walls.

sentences.zh: 可選諸王，使君國典兵，往往棋□寺，鎮撫皇畿，翼亮帝室。

translations.literal: Princes should be selected and made to govern their domains and command troops, dispersed as feudal shields, securing the imperial heartland and supporting the royal house.
translations.idiomatic: Choose princes to hold their states and command troops, set them as shields around the throne, pacify the capital region, and buttress the imperial house.

sentences.zh: 夫皇天無親，惟德是輔。

translations.literal: High Heaven is without partiality; only virtue does it assist.
translations.idiomatic: Heaven shows no favor—it aids the virtuous alone.

sentences.zh: 民詠德政，則延期過歷；

translations.literal: When the people sing of virtuous government, the reign is prolonged beyond its measure;
translations.idiomatic: When the people praise good rule, a dynasty outlasts its span;

sentences.zh: 下有怨歎，則輟錄授能。

translations.literal: when below there is resentment and sighing, the mandate is withdrawn and given to the able.
translations.idiomatic: when they groan beneath injustice, Heaven withdraws the mandate and gives it to another.

sentences.zh: 由此觀之，天下乃天下之天下，非獨陛下之天下也！

translations.literal: From this we see: the realm is the realm of all under Heaven—not Your Majesty's realm alone!
translations.idiomatic: See then: the realm belongs to all under Heaven—not to Your Majesty alone!

sentences.zh: 」帝手詔深慰勞之。

translations.literal: " The emperor wrote back in his own hand, deeply comforting and commending him.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor replied in his own hand with warm praise.

sentences.zh: 未幾而卒。

translations.literal: Before long he died.
translations.idiomatic: Soon after, he died.

sentences.zh: 陳壽評曰：高堂隆學業修明，志存匡君，因變陳戒，發於懇誠，忠矣哉！

translations.literal: Chen Shou commented: Gao Tanglong's learning was cultivated and clear, his will set on correcting the ruler; seizing the moment of omen he offered warning, springing from earnest sincerity—how loyal!
translations.idiomatic: Chen Shou wrote: Gao Tanglong was learned and upright, his heart set on saving his ruler. He seized an omen to speak truth from the depths of sincerity—how loyal!

sentences.zh: 及至必改正朔，俾魏祖虞，所謂意過其通者歟！

translations.literal: Yet when it came to insisting on changing the calendar and making Wei the equal of Yu—this is what is meant by intention exceeding what reason can bear!
translations.idiomatic: Yet in urging a new calendar and ranking Wei with Yu, he overreached—intent outran wisdom.

sentences.zh: 帝深疾浮華之士，詔吏部尚書盧毓曰：「選舉莫取有名，名如畫地作餅，不可啖也。

translations.literal: The emperor deeply detested men of empty show; he edicted to Lu Yu, Minister of the Masters of Writing: "In selection, do not take men for their fame—fame is like drawing a cake on the ground; it cannot be eaten."
translations.idiomatic: The emperor despised hollow reputation. He told Lu Yu, Minister of the Masters of Writing: "Do not choose men for fame alone. Fame is a cake drawn on the ground—it cannot be eaten."

sentences.zh: 」毓對曰：「名不足以致異人而可以得常士：常士畏教慕善，然後有名，非所當疾也。

translations.literal: Yu replied: "Fame is not enough to obtain extraordinary men, yet it can obtain ordinary men: ordinary men fear instruction and admire goodness, and only then have fame—this is not what should be detested.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Yu answered: "Fame will not win you prodigies, but it can win solid men. Ordinary men fear discipline and love virtue—that is how they earn a name. That is no evil."

sentences.zh: 愚臣既不足以識異人，又主者正以循名案常為職，但當有以驗其後耳。

translations.literal: I, your foolish minister, am not enough to recognize extraordinary men, and the chief officials are justly charged with matching names to the regular standard as their duty—only there should be means to verify them afterward.
translations.idiomatic: I am too dull to spot prodigies; your ministers' duty is to match names to records. What matters is to test men after they are chosen.

sentences.zh: 古者敷奏以言，明試以功；

translations.literal: In antiquity memorials were submitted in words and merit was clearly tested in deeds;
translations.idiomatic: Antiquity judged men by memorial and proved them by deeds;

sentences.zh: 今考績之法廢，而以毀譽相進退，故真偽渾雜，虛實相蒙。

translations.literal: today the method of examining achievement is abandoned, and promotion and demotion proceed by praise and blame—thus true and false mingle, empty and full conceal each other.
translations.idiomatic: today performance review is dead, and praise and slander alone decide rank—so truth and pretense blur together.

sentences.zh: 」帝納其言。

translations.literal: " The emperor accepted his words.
translations.idiomatic: The emperor agreed.

sentences.zh: 詔散騎常侍劉邵作考課法。

translations.literal: An edict ordered Palace Attendant Liu Shao to compose a method of examination.
translations.idiomatic: He ordered Palace Attendant Liu Shao to draft an examination law.

sentences.zh: 卲作《都官考課法》七十二條，又作《說略》一篇，詔下百官議。

translations.literal: Shao composed seventy-two articles of the Capital Offices Examination Law, and also one essay called Exposition in Brief; an edict sent them down for discussion among the hundred officials.
translations.idiomatic: Shao wrote seventy-two articles of the Capital Offices Examination Law and a brief exposition; the court circulated both for debate.

sentences.zh: 司隸校尉崔林曰：「案《周官》考課，其文備矣。

translations.literal: Director of the Masters of Writing Cui Lin said: "Examining the Rites of Zhou, its texts on examination are complete.
translations.idiomatic: Cui Lin, Director of the Masters of Writing, said: "The Rites of Zhou set out examination in full.

sentences.zh: 自康王以下，遂以陵夷，此即考課之法存乎其人也。

translations.literal: From King Kang downward it declined by degrees—thus the method of examination survives in the men who hold it.
translations.idiomatic: After King Kang it decayed step by step—the law lived on only in the men who embodied it.

sentences.zh: 及漢之季，其失豈在乎佐吏之職不密哉！

translations.literal: By the end of Han, was its failure really because the duties of assisting officials were not strict!
translations.idiomatic: By Han's end, was the fault truly that clerks' duties were lax?

sentences.zh: 方今軍旅或猥或卒，增減無常，固難一矣。

translations.literal: Today armies in the field are sometimes massed and sometimes rushed, increased or reduced without fixed rule—naturally it is hard to unify them in one measure.
translations.idiomatic: Armies today swell and shrink without pattern—naturally one rule cannot fit all.

sentences.zh: 且萬目不張，舉其綱，眾毛不整，振其領，皋陶仕虞，伊尹臣殷，不仁者遠。

translations.literal: When ten thousand eyes are not open, raise the net; when many hairs are not combed, shake the collar—Gao Yao served Yu, Yi Yin served Yin, and the unworthy kept their distance.
translations.idiomatic: When myriad eyes cannot see, lift the net; when countless hairs tangle, straighten the collar. Gao Yao served Yu, Yi Yin served Yin—and the wicked stood far off.

sentences.zh: 若大臣能任其職，式是百辟，則孰敢不肅，烏在考課哉！

translations.literal: If great ministers can fulfill their duties and take the hundred officials as their model, who would dare not be reverent—where is the need for examination!
translations.idiomatic: If great ministers do their work and lead the hundred offices by example, who will not obey—what need of examinations?

sentences.zh: 」黃門侍郎杜恕曰：「明試以功，三考黜陟，誠帝王之盛制也。

translations.literal: " Yellow Gate Gentleman Du Shu said: "To clearly test by achievement, with three examinations and demotion or promotion—truly this is the sage ruler's grand institution.
translations.idiomatic: Du Shu, Yellow Gate Gentleman, said: "To prove merit by deeds, with three reviews deciding rank—that is the sage ruler's finest institution.

sentences.zh: 然歷六代而考績之法不著，關七聖而課試之文不垂，臣誠以為其法可粗依，其詳難備舉故也。

translations.literal: Yet through six dynasties the method of examining achievement was not set forth; spanning seven sage rulers the texts on examination and testing were not handed down—I truly think its method can be roughly followed, but its details are hard to set forth completely.
translations.idiomatic: Yet six dynasties passed without such a law; seven sage kings left no full text. The principle may be followed, but the details cannot all be set down.

sentences.zh: 語曰『世有亂人而無亂法』，若使法可專任，則唐、虞可不須稷、契之佐，殷、周無貴伊、呂之輔矣。

translations.literal: The saying goes, 'There are disorderly men but no disorderly laws'; if laws alone could be relied on, then Tang and Yu would not have needed Ji and Xie as assistants, and Yin and Zhou would not have prized Yi and Lü as supports.
translations.idiomatic: They say: 'There are wicked men, but no wicked laws.' If law alone sufficed, Tang and Yu would not have needed Ji and Xie, nor Yin and Zhou Yi and Lü.

sentences.zh: 今奏考功者，陳周、漢之雲為，綴京房之本旨，可謂明考課之要矣。

translations.literal: Those who now present the examination of merit cite the cloud-like deeds of Zhou and Han and string together the original intent of Jing Fang—this can be called grasping the essentials of examination.
translations.idiomatic: Those who propose merit review cite Zhou and Han and follow Jing Fang's intent—they grasp the heart of the matter.

sentences.zh: 於以崇揖讓之風，興濟濟之治，臣以為未盡善也。

translations.literal: By this to exalt the wind of yielding and courtesy and raise well-ordered governance—I think it is not yet fully good.
translations.idiomatic: To revive yielding courtesy and ordered rule by this alone—I think it is not yet enough.

sentences.zh: 其欲使州郡考士，必由四科，皆有事效，然後察舉，試辟公府，為新民長吏，轉以功次補郡守者，或就增秩賜爵，此最考課之急務也。

translations.literal: What they wish is that the commanderies and districts examine scholars through the four categories, all with proven service, and only then inspect and recommend them; test them at the public offices, appoint them as new district chiefs and magistrates, and promote them in order of merit to commandery administrators—or at once raise rank and bestow nobility—this is the most urgent task of examination.
translations.idiomatic: They would have districts test scholars by four ranks, with proven service, before recommendation; try them in office, appoint them as magistrates, and promote by merit to prefect—or raise rank and ennoble them at once. That is the urgent core of review.

sentences.zh: 臣以為便當顯其身，用其言，使具為課州郡之法，法具施行，立必信之賞，施必行之罰。

translations.literal: I think they should at once make their persons conspicuous, employ their words, and have them fully draft the law for examining commanderies and districts; when the law is complete and put into effect, establish rewards sure to be believed and punishments sure to be carried out.
translations.idiomatic: Let them stand forth, use their counsel, and draft the district examination law in full. When it is ready, grant rewards that will be trusted and punishments that will be enforced.

sentences.zh: 至於公卿及內職大臣，亦當俱以其職考課之。

translations.literal: As for chief ministers and inner-court great ministers, they too should be examined according to their offices.
translations.idiomatic: Grand ministers and inner-court officers should be examined by their offices as well.

sentences.zh: 古之三公，坐而論道；

translations.literal: The Three Excellencies of old sat and discoursed on the Way;
translations.idiomatic: The Three Excellencies of old sat and spoke of the Way;

sentences.zh: 內職大臣，納言補闕，無善不紀，無過不舉。

translations.literal: inner-court great ministers remonstrated and supplied what was lacking—no good went unrecorded, no fault went unreported.
translations.idiomatic: inner ministers remonstrated and filled what was missing—no good unrecorded, no fault unreported.

sentences.zh: 且天下至大，萬機至眾，誠非一明所能遍照；

translations.literal: Moreover, the realm is vast and myriad affairs numerous—truly it is not something one bright man can illuminate everywhere;
translations.idiomatic: The realm is vast and affairs countless—not one bright man can see all;

sentences.zh: 故君為元首，臣作股肱，明其一體相須而成也。

translations.literal: therefore the ruler is the head and ministers are the arms and legs—clearly one body needing each other to be complete.
translations.idiomatic: therefore the ruler is the head and ministers the limbs—one body that must work together to stand.

sentences.zh: 是以古人稱廊廟之材，非一木之枝，帝王之業，非一士之略。

translations.literal: Therefore the ancients called talent for the court and temple not a single branch of a tree, and the enterprise of emperors and kings not the strategy of one man.
translations.idiomatic: Therefore the ancients said that court and temple depend on more than one branch, and an emperor's work on more than one man's plan.

sentences.zh: 由是言之，焉有大臣守職辦課，可以致雍熙者哉！

translations.literal: From this we speak: how could there be great ministers who merely keep office and handle examinations and thereby bring about great peace!
translations.idiomatic: From this it follows: how could ministers who only keep their posts and run examinations bring the realm to flourishing peace!

sentences.zh: 誠使容身保位，無放退之辜，而盡節在公，抱見疑之勢，公義不修而私議成欲，雖仲尼為課，猶不能盡一才，又況於世俗之人乎！

translations.literal: If they truly only secure their persons and preserve position without fault of dismissal, yet give full loyalty in public service while embracing the posture of being suspected, not cultivating public righteousness while private talk fulfills desire—even if Confucius conducted the examination, he still could not exhaust one man's talent, how much more the men of the vulgar world!
translations.idiomatic: If men only cling to office without demotion, yet serve in public while living under suspicion, neglecting justice while private talk rules desire—even Confucius as examiner could not measure one man's worth, still less ordinary men!

sentences.zh: 」司空掾北地傅嘏曰：「夫建官均職，清理民物，所以立本也。

translations.literal: " Fu Gu, aide to the Minister of Works from Beidi, said: "To establish offices and balance duties, to order and clarify the people's affairs—this is to set the root.
translations.idiomatic: Fu Gu, aide to the Minister of Works, said, "To establish offices and balance duties and order the people's affairs is to set the root.

sentences.zh: 循名考實，糾勵成規，所以治末也。

translations.literal: To follow names and examine realities, to correct and encourage completed standards—this is to govern the branch.
translations.idiomatic: To match names to deeds and enforce standards is to govern the branches.

sentences.zh: 本綱未舉而造制末程，國略不崇而考課是先，懼不足以料賢愚之分，精幽明之理也。

translations.literal: If the root's net is not raised yet one hastens to make the branch's measure, if the state's grand design is not exalted yet examination comes first—I fear it is not enough to distinguish wise from foolish or to refine the principles of the hidden and the manifest.
translations.idiomatic: If the root is neglected while branch rules are rushed, if national strategy is set aside while examinations come first—I fear you cannot tell sage from fool, nor weigh what is hidden against what is clear.

sentences.zh: 」議久之不決，事竟不行。

translations.literal: " Discussion went on long without decision, and the matter in the end was not carried out.
translations.idiomatic: Debate dragged on, and in the end nothing was done.

sentences.zh: 臣光曰：為治之要，莫先於用人，而知人之道，聖賢所難也。

translations.literal: Your servant Guang remarks: The essential of governing lies first in employing men, and the way to know men is what sages and worthies find difficult.
translations.idiomatic: Sima Guang comments: The heart of government is employing the right people, and knowing people is what even sages find hard.

sentences.zh: 是故求之於毀譽，則愛憎競進而善惡渾殽；

translations.literal: Therefore, if one seeks them in praise and blame, love and hatred race forward and good and evil are mingled in confusion;
translations.idiomatic: Seek them in gossip, and love and hatred tangle good with evil;

sentences.zh: 考之於功狀，則巧詐橫生而真偽相冒。

translations.literal: if one examines them in records of achievement, craft and deceit arise in swarms and true and false conceal each other.
translations.idiomatic: judge them by paperwork, and craft and deceit swarm until truth and falsehood blur.

sentences.zh: 要之，其本在於至公至明而已矣。

translations.literal: In sum, the root lies in utmost fairness and utmost clarity alone.
translations.idiomatic: In the end, the root is nothing but perfect fairness and perfect clarity.

sentences.zh: 為人上者至公至明，則群下之能否焯然形於目中，無所復逃矣。

translations.literal: If one above others is utterly fair and utterly clear, then the ability or inability of those below stands out clearly before the eyes and none can escape.
translations.idiomatic: A ruler utterly fair and clear sees every subordinate's strength or weakness plain before him, and none can hide.

sentences.zh: 苟為不公不明，則考課之法，適足以為曲私欺罔之資也。

translations.literal: If one is not fair and not clear, then the method of examination becomes precisely the resource for crooked favoritism and deceit.
translations.idiomatic: If he is neither fair nor clear, examination laws become tools for favoritism and fraud.

sentences.zh: 何以言之？

translations.literal: How do we say this?
translations.idiomatic: Why is that?

sentences.zh: 公明者，心也；

translations.literal: Fairness and clarity are the mind;
translations.idiomatic: Fairness and clarity are in the mind;

sentences.zh: 功狀者，跡也。

translations.literal: records of achievement are the traces.
translations.idiomatic: records of achievement are only traces.

sentences.zh: 己之心不能治，而以考人之跡，不亦難乎！

translations.literal: If one's own mind cannot be governed, yet one examines others' traces—is it not difficult!
translations.idiomatic: If you cannot govern your own mind, yet judge others by their traces—is that not hard?

sentences.zh: 為人上者，誠能不以親疏貴賤異其心，喜怒好惡亂其志，欲知治經之士，則視其記覽博洽，講論精通，斯為善治經矣；

translations.literal: If one above others can truly not let closeness or distance, nobility or baseness alter the mind, nor let pleasure, anger, love, or hatred disorder the will—to know men who govern the classics, then observe whether their learning is broad and their discourse masterful: that is one who governs the classics well;
translations.idiomatic: If a ruler will not let kinship, rank, pleasure, or anger sway him—to find a classicist, see whether his learning is broad and his exposition masterful;

sentences.zh: 欲知治獄之士，則視其曲盡情偽，無所冤抑，斯為善治獄矣；

translations.literal: to know men who govern punishments, then observe whether they exhaust feeling and falsity and have no wrongful suppression: that is one who governs punishments well;
translations.idiomatic: to find a jurist, see whether he weighs every circumstance and never wrongfully condemns;

sentences.zh: 欲知治財之士，則視其倉庫盈產，百姓富給，斯為善治財矣；

translations.literal: to know men who govern finances, then observe whether the granaries are full and the people are rich and provided: that is one who governs finances well;
translations.idiomatic: to find a treasurer, see whether the stores are full and the people prosper;

sentences.zh: 欲知治兵之士，則視其戰勝攻取，敵人畏服，斯為善治兵矣。

translations.literal: to know men who govern armies, then observe whether they conquer in battle and attack and the enemy fears and submits: that is one who governs armies well.
translations.idiomatic: to find a commander, see whether he wins in the field and the enemy fears him.

sentences.zh: 至於百官，莫不皆然。

translations.literal: As for the hundred offices, none is not likewise.
translations.idiomatic: The same holds for every office.

sentences.zh: 雖詢謀於人而決之在己，雖考求於跡而察之在心，研核其實而斟酌其宜，至精至微，不可以口述，不可以書傳也，安得豫為之法而悉委有司哉！

translations.literal: Though one consults others yet decides in oneself, though one examines traces yet inspects in the mind, sifting the reality and weighing what is fitting—so refined and so subtle it cannot be told by mouth or handed down in writing: how can one pre-make a law and wholly entrust it to the responsible offices!
translations.idiomatic: Though you consult others, you decide yourself; though you read records, you judge in your heart—sifting truth, weighing fitness, too fine for speech or script. How can you pre-write a law and leave it all to clerks?

sentences.zh: 或者親貴雖不能而任職，疏賤雖賢才而見遺；

translations.literal: Perhaps the close and noble, though unable, still hold office, while the distant and base, though talented, are passed over;
translations.idiomatic: Kin may hold office without ability; the distant and humble may be passed over though able;

sentences.zh: 所喜所好者敗官而不去，所怒所惡者有功而不錄，詢謀於人，則毀譽相半而不能決；

translations.literal: those one likes and loves ruin their posts yet are not removed, those one hates and detests have merit yet are not recorded; when consulting others, praise and blame are half and half and one cannot decide;
translations.idiomatic: favorites who fail remain, men you hate though worthy go unrewarded; ask the court and hear only half-truths;

sentences.zh: 考求於跡，則文具實亡而不能察。

translations.literal: when examining traces, the documents exist but the reality is gone and one cannot discern.
translations.idiomatic: read the files and find form without substance.

sentences.zh: 雖復為之善法，繁其條目，謹其簿書，安能得其真哉！

translations.literal: Even if one again makes a good law, multiplies its articles, and is strict with its ledgers—how can one obtain the truth!
translations.idiomatic: Even perfect laws and meticulous ledgers cannot yield the truth!

sentences.zh: 或曰：人君之治，大者天下，小者一國，內外之官以千萬數，考察黜陟，安得不委有司而獨任其事哉？

translations.literal: Someone may say: In a ruler's governance, the large is the realm, the small is one state; officials within and without number in the tens of millions—how in examining, demoting, and promoting can one not entrust it to the responsible offices and bear the affair alone?
translations.idiomatic: One may ask: A realm has millions of officials—how can promotion and demotion not be delegated?

sentences.zh: 曰：非謂其然也。

translations.literal: The reply is: That is not what is meant.
translations.idiomatic: The answer is: That is not what is meant.

sentences.zh: 凡為人上者，不特人君而已。

translations.literal: All who are above others are not only the ruler.
translations.idiomatic: Every superior is not only a Son of Heaven.

sentences.zh: 太守居一郡之上，刺史居一州之上，九卿居屬官之上，三公居百執事之上，皆用此道以考察黜陟在下之人，為人君者亦用此道以考察黜陟公卿、刺史、太守，奚煩勞之有哉！

translations.literal: A grand administrator presides over a commandery, an inspector over a province, the Nine Ministers over their subordinates, the Three Excellencies over the hundred executors—all use this Way to examine, demote, and promote those below; the ruler also uses this Way to examine, demote, and promote the chief ministers, inspectors, and grand administrators—what trouble or labor is there!
translations.idiomatic: A prefect, an inspector, a minister, a chancellor—each uses this same way on those below; the emperor uses it on them. Where is the burden?

sentences.zh: 或曰：考績之法，唐、虞所為，京房、劉邵述而修之耳，烏可廢哉？

translations.literal: Someone may say: The method of examining achievement is what Tang and Yu did; Jing Fang and Liu Shao merely elaborated and repaired it—how can it be abandoned!
translations.idiomatic: Another may say: Tang and Yu examined merit; Jing Fang and Liu Shao only codified it—how abolish it?

sentences.zh: 曰：唐、虞之官，其居位也久，其受任也專，其立法也寬，其責成也遠。

translations.literal: The reply is: The officials of Tang and Yu held position long, received appointment exclusively, made law lenient, and held achievement accountable from afar.
translations.idiomatic: The reply: Tang and Yu's officers served long and solely, laws were lenient, and accountability was distant.

sentences.zh: 是故鯀之治水，九載績用弗成，然後治其罪；

translations.literal: Therefore Gun's control of the waters—nine years' achievement unfulfilled—and only then was his crime punished;
translations.idiomatic: Gun labored nine years on the flood without success—only then was he punished;

sentences.zh: 禹之治水，九州攸同，四隩既宅，然後賞其功；

translations.literal: Yu controlled the waters—the nine regions were alike, the four frontiers were settled—and only then was his merit rewarded;
translations.idiomatic: Yu tamed the flood until the nine regions were ordered—only then was he rewarded;

sentences.zh: 非若京房、劉邵之法，校其米鹽之課，責其旦夕之效也。

translations.literal: this is not like the method of Jing Fang and Liu Shao, checking the accounts of rice and salt and demanding achievement within the morning and evening.
translations.idiomatic: not like Jing Fang and Liu Shao, who count rice and salt and demand results by nightfall.

sentences.zh: 事固有名同而實異者，不可不察也。

translations.literal: Affairs indeed have the same name yet different reality—this cannot go unexamined.
translations.idiomatic: Names may match, yet realities differ—that must be weighed.

sentences.zh: 考績非可行於唐、虞而不可行於漢、魏，由京房、劉邵不得其本而奔趨其末故也。

translations.literal: Examination of achievement is not that it could be practiced in Tang and Yu yet not in Han and Wei; it is because Jing Fang and Liu Shao did not obtain the root and rushed to the branch.
translations.idiomatic: Merit review failed in Han and Wei not because it could not work, but because Jing Fang and Liu Shao seized the branch and missed the root.

sentences.zh: 初，右僕射衛臻典選舉，中護軍蔣濟遺臻書曰：「漢祖遇亡虜為上將，周武拔漁父為太師，布衣廝養，可登王公，何必守文，試而後用！

translations.literal: Earlier, Right Vice Director Wei Zhen oversaw selection; Central Protector of the Army Jiang Ji sent Zhen a letter, saying: "Han's founder met a surrendered barbarian and made him grand general; Zhou's martial king drew a fisherman and made him Grand Tutor—commoners and menials can ascend to king and duke; why must one keep to precedent and try before employing!"
translations.idiomatic: Earlier, Wei Zhen oversaw appointments; Jiang Ji wrote him: "Gaozu made a surrendered barbarian his general; King Wu of Zhou made a fisherman his Grand Tutor—why insist on precedent and trial before use?"

sentences.zh: 」臻曰：「不然。

translations.literal: " Zhen said: "Not so.
translations.idiomatic: Zhen replied, "Not so.

sentences.zh: 子欲同牧野於成、康，喻斷蛇於文、景，好不經之舉，開拔奇之津，將使天下馳騁而起矣！

translations.literal: You would equate Muye with the age of Cheng and Kang, and compare the severed snake with Wen and Jing—favoring unorthodox appointments and opening the ford for plucking the extraordinary will make all under Heaven gallop forth at once!
translations.idiomatic: You would liken Muye to the age of Cheng and Kang, and a serpent omen to Wen and Jing—open the gate to eccentric choice and the realm will rush to chaos!

sentences.zh: 」盧毓論人及選舉，皆先性行而後言才，黃門郎馮翊李豐嘗以問毓，毓曰：「才所以為善也，故大才成大善，小才成小善。

translations.literal: Lu Yu in discussing men and selection always put conduct first and talent in words after; Li Feng, Gentleman of the Yellow Gate from Fufeng, once questioned Yu about this.
translations.idiomatic: Lu Yu always weighed character before talent in appointments; Li Feng of Fufeng once asked him about this.

sentences.zh: 今稱之有才而不能為善，是才不中器也！

translations.literal: Yu said: "Talent is the means to goodness; therefore great talent achieves great good, small talent achieves small good.
translations.idiomatic: Yu said, "Talent is the vessel for goodness—great talent yields great good, small talent small good.

sentences.zh: 」豐服其言。

translations.literal: Now to call one talented yet unable to do good—that is talent not fitting the vessel!"
translations.idiomatic: To praise talent that produces no good is to praise a vessel that cannot hold water!"
